Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
NDY=Number of days in the year
AA=Availability achieved during the month including Deemed Availability,
Monthly Energy Charge is defined in Clause 1.2.3 of Schedule F, as
extracted hereunder:-
“1.2.3. Monthly Energy Charges
The Monthly Energy Charge Payment for any month in a Year shall be
calculated as below:
Energy charge rate in Rs./kWh x scheduled energy (ex-bus) for the month
in kWh.
Energy charge rate (ECR) in Rupees per kWh on ex-power plant basis shall
be the sum of energy charge rate as determined by the Commission as per
the Tariff Regulations which may be computed to three decimal places in
accordance with the following formulae and Fuel Cost Adjustment:
ECR= [ {(SHR-SFC x CVSF) x LPPF / CVPF+LPSF x SFC) x 100/ (100-
AUX)] +FCA
Where,
AUX=Normative auxiliary energy consumption as per Prescribed
Parameters CVPFGross Calorific Value of coal as fired, in kCal per kg to
be calculated as given below:
Initially, Gross Calorific Value of coal shall be taken as per actual of the
preceding three months. Any variation shall be adjusted on month to month
basis on the basis of Gross Calorific Value of coal received and burnt and
landed cost incurred by the Company for procurement of coal.
CVSF=Calorific value of secondary fuel, in kCal per ml.
SHR=Station Heat Rate, in kCal per kWh.
LPP= Weighted average landed price of primary fuel i.e. coal, in Rupees
per kg during the month.
LPSF=Weighted average landed cost of Secondary fuel oil in Rs/ml
SFC=Normative Specific fuel oil consumption as per Prescribed
Parameters
Page 11 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
The landed cost of fuel for the month shall include price of fuel
corresponding to the grade and quality of fuel inclusive of royalty, taxes
and duties as applicable, Washery charges as applicable, transportation
cost by rail/ road or any other means, and, for the purpose of computation
of energy charge, and shall be arrived at after considering normative transit
and handling losses for coal of 0.8% of the quantity of coal dispatched by
the coal supply company during the month.
iii. APERC Regulations 2008;
As per Regulation 11.1.1, the Target Availability for full recovery of
Annual fixed charges in case of coal/gas base plants is set as 80 % . In
these Regulations, the Components for annual fixed charges are Return
on Capital Employed, Depreciation, taxes on Income and O&M
expenses as defined in Regulation 12 and their recovery is related to
Target Availability. Energy Charge Computation is defined in Regulation
13 and formula for the same is extracted as under:
Energy Charge (Rs) = rate of Energy Charge in Rs /kwh)x Ex-bus energy
sent out corresponding to scheduled energy for the month in kwh.
13. It is clear from the above that 85 % normative availability for Appellant’s
plant is in accordance with CERC norms as adopted by State Commission in
its order dated 01.08.2022, because APERC Regulations stipulates normative
availability of 80 %. It is also clear from the above, that the governing
framework, whether under the CERC Regulations, the APERC Regulations, or
the Power Purchase Agreement executed between the parties expressly
stipulates the methodology for recovery of monthly charges. The scheme is
clear and unambiguous: monthly fixed charges are linked to the Plant
Availability Factor (PAF) for the month vis-à-vis the normative annual plant
Page 12 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
availability, whereas energy charges are linked solely to the fuel cost/energy
charge pertaining to the quantum of energy actually supplied during the month.
14. CERC Regulations as well PPA provide that in the event, generator fails to
achieve the targeted availability, there shall be a penalty in the monthly fixed
capacity charges. Simultaneously, the payment of monthly energy charges is
limited strictly to recovery of fuel charges for the energy supplied, irrespective
of the plant availability in that month. Thus, the regulatory and contractual
scheme draws a clear distinction: fixed charges are availability-linked, subject
to penalty for shortfall, whereas energy charges are supply-linked, confined to
reimbursement of actual fuel cost.
15. It is submitted on behalf of State Commission that the Denial/reduction of
Capacity Charges for availability shortfalls accounts for the generator's lost
fixed-cost recovery but it does not compensate DISCOMs or consumers for
the additional burden of forced higher-cost procurement from the market, to
replace the shortfall in energy from the Appellant. The deductions from
Variable Charges provide partial compensation for these avoidable costs and
serve as a direct disincentive against chronic monthly under performance.
Accordingly, the main issue is whether APERC, while determining tariff, can
regulate instances of drastic and unpredictable monthly availability shortfall by
generators even in the circumstances where such generators largely meet
their annual availability requirements. It is submitted on behalf of Respondents
that while the PPA and Regulations focus on annual normative availability, they
do not preclude monthly adjustments. According to the Respondents, APERC,
being a statutory body, is empowered and obligated to fill contractual and
regulatory gaps to ensure reliable supply. The Respondents placed reliance
Page 13 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
on the Supreme Court Judgements; “PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, (2010) 4 SCC
603”, “Power Grid Corporation of India Limited vs. Madhya Pradesh
Power Transmission Company Limited & Ors., (2025) 8 SCC 705” to
support their contentions with regard to imposition of graded deductions on
variable charges. State Commission submit that under Sections 62 and 86 of
the Electricity Act, 2003, APERC has broad statutory powers to determine
tariffs, including specifying incentive/penalty structures for performance
metrics such as availability, even when Regulations are silent on the specific
matter.
16. Some force may be found in the submissions advanced on behalf of the
Respondents, to the effect that mere reduction in fixed cost recovery for failure
to achieve the targeted availability in a month may not adequately compensate
or offset the financial burden occasioned by procurement of costly short-term
power, and therefore a penalty by way of reduction in the variable
charge/energy charge could appear justifiable. However, such considerations
of equity or expediency cannot prevail in a regulated framework. In a statutory
regulatory regime, the Commission is bound to act strictly in accordance with
the governing provisions of the Act.
17. The scheme of recovery of fixed cost and energy charge in a given month
is prescribed by the Regulation itself. Once the Regulation stipulates the
manner in which fixed cost is to be recovered, and the manner in which energy
charge is to be computed and levied, the Commission has no jurisdiction to
interfere with or modify that scheme by way of adjudication or in a tariff order.
Any departure from the prescribed mechanism can only be effected by way of
Page 14 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
a formal amendment to the Regulation in accordance with law, and not
otherwise.
18. Accordingly, although the grievance of the Respondents may have some
practical appeal, the State Commission cannot substitute its own view for the
statutory prescription. The recovery of fixed cost and energy charge must be
effected strictly in the manner laid down in the applicable Regulation, and any
penalty or disallowance must be confined to the mode expressly provided
therein. Moreover, in the present case PPA also stipulates the same
methodology as stipulated in the Regulations for recovery of monthly energy
charge delinked with the availability achieved in that month. Therefore we don’t
find any merit in the contention of State Commission that Appellant has been
granted liberty to approach the Commission with a petition if the shortfall is for
reasons beyond their Control.
19. It is further evident from the foregoing discussion that the CERC
Regulations framed under Section 181 of the Electricity Act, 2003, were
adopted for the Appellant’s plant and as such both CERC as well as APERC
Regulations clearly stipulate the methodology for recovery of energy charges
for a given month. Once such methodology is prescribed, the Commission is
bound to apply it in its entirety. We therefore, find no merit in the submission
of the Respondents that there exists a gap in the regulatory scheme which the
State Commission, as a statutory body, is empowered or obligated to fill in
order to ensure reliable supply. The doctrine of casus omissus has no
application in the present context, for the Regulations are complete in
themselves and leave no vacuum for the Commission to legislate by way of
adjudication.
Page 15 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
20. We may also observe that the application of similar reduction in energy
charges for other intra-State generators by the State Commission is of no
relevance in the present proceedings. Those orders are not under challenge
before us, and this Tribunal is not bound to apply the same principle in the
case of the Appellant merely because it has been applied elsewhere. Each
appeal must be adjudicated on the basis of the statutory framework and the
specific impugned order under consideration. The doctrine of parity cannot be
invoked to perpetuate an illegality or to justify a deviation from the Regulations.
21. In consequence, we hold that the reasoning adopted by the State
Commission in the impugned order, as well as it seeks to justify reduction of
energy charges by reference to similar treatment accorded to other intra-State
generators, is unsustainable in law.
22. The reliance placed by the Respondents on the ratio of PTC India Ltd. v.
CERC, (2010) 4 SCC 603 and Power Grid Corporation of India Limited v.
Madhya Pradesh Power Transmission Company Limited & Ors., (2025) 8
SCC 705 is wholly misplaced. Those decisions dealt with the binding nature
of regulations and the scope of regulatory powers in different contexts. They
do not advance the Respondents’ contention that the Commission may, in the
guise of filling contractual or regulatory gaps, alter the express methodology
prescribed for recovery of charges. In the present case, the Regulations
themselves provide the governing framework, and the Commission is
duty-bound to adhere to them.
Page 16 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
23. We hold that the findings recorded in the Impugned Order on this issue
cannot be sustained in law. The Commission’s attempt to deviate from the
prescribed methodology of recovery of energy charges, under the pretext of
filling an alleged regulatory gap, is ultra vires the Regulations and contrary to
settled principles of delegated legislation. It is settled position that once the
methodology is expressly prescribed in Regulations, the same is required to
be applied in its entirety.
24. In view of above deliberations, the findings in the Impugned Order on the
issue cannot be sustained in law and need to be set aside and the Appellant
is entitled for refund of the amount withheld/deducted from the energy charge
along with applicable carrying cost as per Regulations.
ISSUE B: PART LOAD COMPENSATION
25. It is submitted on behalf of the Appellant that the provisions of CERC
Regulations (4th Amendment to the Grid Code), the applicability whereof to
the Appellant has been determined by the State Commission vide its Order
dated 01.08.2022, specifically provides for Part load compensation (PLC). The
Appellant further submits that its claim towards PLC claim is in accordance
with the Detailed Procedure as approved by CERC vide order dated
05.05.2017. However, the Impugned Order contains no discussion, analysis,
or finding on the PLC claim.
26. It is admitted on behalf of the Respondent Discom that Revised
Consolidated PPA, entered into between the Appellant and DISCOMs
explicitly provides for part load compensation. The Respondents have further
submitted that PLC pertaining to the previous Control Period has been claimed
Page 17 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
as a part of True-Up process on actuals basis and therefore, no separate
determination was required in the framework of multi-year tariff and ARR vide
Impugned order. It has also been contended that no claim towards PLC had
been raised by the Appellant.
27. We note from the Schedule-F of the PPA dated 16.07.2024 that Monthly
Part Load Compensation is required to be computed in accordance with the
Grid Code as notified by CERC, relevant clause is extracted hereunder:
“1.2.5. Monthly Part load Compensation Charges: Monthly Part
Load Compensation Charges shall be computed in accordance with
CERC (Indian Electricity Grid Code) (Fourth Amendment)
Regulations, 2016, notified on 6th April 2016, as amended from
time to time.”
28. In the Impugned Order, State Commission has recorded the submissions
of Appellant that it was claiming Part Load Compensation from the Discoms in
terms of Clause 1.2.5 of Schedule-F of the PPA read with Regulation 6.3B of
IEGC (fourth amendment), 2016.
29. In view of these submissions/acknowledgment by Respondents, there
seems to be no dispute with regard to the entitlement of the Appellant for Part
Load Compensation. Accordingly, the Appellant is entitled to part load
compensation in terms of the provision of the PPA executed between the
Appellant and Discom and to claim the same as per Regulation 6.3B of the
IEGC (fourth Amendment) 2016 as amended from time to time.
30. We further note from the Petition filed by Appellant before State
Commission that the Appellant has claimed part load compensation amounting
Page 18 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 27 of 2026
to Rs 119,12,56,167 (excluding carrying cost) from the AP Discoms and has
attached letter written to AP Discoms, and Appellant has also asserted that the
said claim was never disputed by the Respondents. However, it is not clear
from the submissions on record whether such an amount has already been
paid or continues to remain outstanding. Since, the issue itself is not under
the dispute, the controversy, if any, appears to be confined only to
quantification and reconciliation of the amount payable/paid, we deem it
appropriate and in the interest of justice to remand the matter to the State
Commission for determination and finalization of the amount payable towards
Part Load Compensation in accordance with the applicable Regulations.
CONCLUSION
In view of above deliberations, two issues are decided as under:
A) Deductions from Variable Charges for shortfall in monthly availability;
the Impugned order is set aside on this issue and recovery of energy
charges to be enforced strictly in accordance with the applicable CERC
Regulations and the stipulations contain in the PPA. The Respondents are
directed to refund the amount deducted/withheld from the energy bills along
with applicable carrying cost in terms of Regulation within the period of four
weeks from the date of this judgement.

1. The present batch of Appeals have been filed by Himachal Pradesh Power
Corporation Limited (“the Appellant”), assailing the orders dated 05.06.2024
(herein referred as “Impugned Orders”) passed by Himachal Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “HPERC/State
Commission”). The Impugned Orders pertains to the approval of capital cost,
including additional capitalization, and determination of tariff from the Commercial
Operation Date (“COD”) up to FY 2023–24 for three projects ( Sainj HEP – 2x50
MW, Kashang –I HEP 1x65 MW and Sawra Kuddu HEP – 3x37 MW) . The details
of the present Appeals are set out hereinbelow:

2024 for 2 X 50 MW Sainj Hydro Electric Project
2. 94 of 2025 Assailing Order dated 05.06.2024 in Petition No. 24 of

3. 135 of 2025 Assailing Order dated 05.06.2024 in Petition No. 26 of

DESCRIPTION OF PARTIES:

3. Respondent No 1 is the Himachal Pradesh Electricity Regulatory

the powers and discharging the functions under the provisions of Electricity Act,
2003.
4. Respondent No 2, the Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd.
(“HPSEBL”) is formed after the reorganization of erstwhile Himachal Pradesh

distribution licensee operating in the State of Himachal Pradesh.
Factual matrix of the Case:
5. The Appellant has developed three hydroelectric projects in Himachal
Pradesh under the Himachal Pradesh Clean Energy Development Investment
Program funded by the Asian Development Bank (“ADB”). The details of the said

i. Sainj HEP (100 MW – 2x50 MW) in District Kullu. Both units

HPERC as 04.09.2017.
ii. Kashang HEP (195 MW – 3x65 MW) in District Kinnaur. Units 1,
2 & 3 achieved actual COD on 31.03.2017, 01.09.2016 and

6. On 29.03.2023, a long-term PPAs were executed between HPPCL and
HPSEBL for sale of 100% of net saleable energy from Kashang HEP Stage-I
(1x65 MW), 50% of net saleable energy from Sainj HEP (2x50 MW), and 100%
of net saleable energy from Sawra Kuddu HEP ( 3x37 MW), effective 01.04.2023
till the useful life of the projects. The remaining 50% power from Sainj HEP was
tied up for sale to the World Bank.
7. HPPCL filed petitions No. 24 of 2024 on 24.06.2023 (Kashang HEP-1x65
MW), Petition No 26 of 2024 (Sawra Kuddu HEP-2x50MW) & Petition No 25 of
2024 (Sainj HEP-3x37MW) on 03.06.2023 seeking approval of capital cost,
additional capitalization and determination of tariff for these three HEPs from
COD to FY 2023-24.

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
8. HPERC passed the Impugned Tariff Orders dated 05.06.2024 determining
capital cost and aggregate revenue requirement for all three HEPs. The approved
capital cost after deduction of 90% of the GoHP Loan is Rs. 357.83 crore for
Kashang HEP, Rs. 436.89 crore for Sainj HEP, and Rs. 942.18 crore for Sawra
Kuddu HEP.
9. HPPCL filed review petitions challenging the Impugned Tariff Orders on the
issue of HPERC treating 90% of the GoHP Loan as a ‘grant’ instead of loan and
deducting the same from the project capital cost for computation of debt, equity,
depreciation, return on equity, interest and financing charges. HPERC dismissed
the review petitions on 05.11.2024 for Kashang and Sainj HEPs and on
19.11.2024 for Sawra Kuddu HEP.
10. Aggrieved by the findings in the Impugned Tariff Orders and Review Orders,
HPPCL has filed the present appeals.
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
11. The Appellant has raised several issues in all the three appeals, however
the issue of treatment of 90% of the GoHP Loan as ‘grant’ and its deduction from
capital cost for tariff determination is common to all three appeals. At the outset
it was submitted by Learned Counsel for the Appellant that present appeals may
be confined to the aspect of consideration of loan to the Appellant Company as
grant and liberty may be granted to raise balance issues by way of separate
Appeals.
Since, the only issue i.e “treatment of 90% of GoHP Loan amount as Grant and
deduction of the same from Capital Cost for computation of tariff” to be
Page 7 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
adjudicated in all the three appeals is common, all the three appeals are disposed
of by this common judgement. Accordingly, we heard Mr. Vishrov Mukharjee,
learned Counsel for the Appellant, Mr. Pradeep Mishra, learned counsel on behalf
of Respondent No 1- State Commission and Mr. Anand Ganeshan, learned
counsel on behalf of Respondent No 2-HPSEBL, written submissions filed by
parties and Impugned Order and other documents relevant for adjudicating the
issue.
Submissions Urged on behalf of Appellant
12. Learned counsel for the Appellant submitted that on 10.09.2008, the
Government of India (“GoI”) entered into a Framework Financing Agreement with
the Asian Development Bank (“ADB”), whereby ADB agreed to extend a
multilateral/multi-tranche financing facility amounting to USD 800 million to GoI
under the Himachal Pradesh Clean Energy Development Investment Program.
13. On 10.11.2008, The GoI and ADB executed a Loan Agreement for Tranche-
1 inter alia for civil works pertaining to one unit (65 MW) and the common
powerhouse for all units of Kashang HEP. Under the said Loan Agreement, ADB
agreed to lend an amount of USD 150 million to GoI with a repayment tenure of
20 years along with a grace period commencing from 10.11.2008 to 15.10.2013,
with the last instalment being payable on 15.04.2033. The said agreement further
provided that GoI shall pay interest to ADB at LIBOR + 0.60%, less a credit of
0.40%, on a semi-annual basis.
14. It is submitted that the said Loan Agreement specifically contemplated that
the proceeds of the loan would be made available by GoI to the Govt of Himachal
Pradesh (GoHP) and, thereafter, the GoHP to make available an amount of USD
147 million, being approximately 98% of the total loan amount, to HPPCL under
Page 8 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
arm’s length on-lending arrangements acceptable to both ADB and GoI. The
agreement further stipulated that the rights and obligations arising out of the On-
Lending Agreements could neither be assigned, amended, abrogated nor waived
except with the satisfaction and approval of ADB and GoI.
15. In furtherance of the policy of the GoI aimed at encouraging investment and
promoting development in special category states such as Himachal Pradesh,
the loan amounts received from ADB were released by GoI to the Government of
Himachal Pradesh on concessional terms, wherein 90% of the financial
assistance was treated as grant and the remaining 10% was treated as loan.
16. Subsequently, GoHP executed an On-Lending Agreement with HPPCL,
which specifically notes that GoI had obtained a loan facility of USD 800 million
from the ADB for financing part of the cost of Kashang, Sainj, Sawra Kuddu and
Shongng Karcham Hydro Electric Projects, and that the loan proceeds would be
transferred by GoI to GoHP, which would further transfer the same to HPPCL.
The said Agreement further provided that GoHP would make available the said
funds to HPPCL by way of a loan carrying simple interest at the rate of 10% per
annum, with interest being payable annually on or before 15th January of each
financial year and the repayment obligation towards interest commencing
immediately. It is also stipulated that HPPCL would repay the principal amount of
each tranche of the loan within a period of 10 years from the expiry of the
applicable grace period of 5 years, tranche-wise. The Agreement additionally
provided that GoHP would remain responsible for repayment of the loan to
GoI/ADB and that HPPCL would bear no direct liability towards GoI or ADB in that
regard.
Page 9 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
17. However, the State Commission in the Impugned Orders has deducted the
GoHP Loan amount from the approved Capital cost of the projects, which is ex
facie contrary to Regulations 10-C, 11 and 26(1) & (2) of the Hydro Tariff
Regulations, 2011. It is submitted that the amounts released by the GoHP to
HPPCL were not in the nature of consumer contribution, grant or subsidy, but
constituted a loan arrangement, inasmuch as the said amounts were repayable
by HPPCL together with interest at the rate of 10% per annum.
18. It is submitted that even pursuant to the Impugned Tariff Orders, HPPCL
wrote to GoHP highlighting the severe financial implications arising from the
Impugned Orders and requested either conversion of the GoHP loan into grant
or issuance of appropriate directions under Section 108 of the Electricity Act to
HPERC for treating the said amount as loan. However, vide letter dated
19.03.2025, GoHP rejected the said request and categorically reiterated that the
financial assistance extended to HPPCL would continue to be treated as a loan
and not as a grant.
19. Subsequently, GoHP continued to demand payments from HPPCL towards
the said loan, and HPPCL, in compliance thereof, made substantial payments
towards interest on the loan, including approximately Rs. 290.20 Crore paid as
on 31.12.2024. Vide letter dated 27.06.2025, GoHP directed HPSEB to adjust an
amount of Rs. 324.52 Crores, being the interest due from HPPCL, against the
subsidy payable by GoHP to HPSEB. Thereafter, on 24.10.2025 and 28.11.2025,
HPPCL made further payments aggregating to Rs. 500 Crore towards interest on
the said loan.
20. It is submitted that Section 61(d) of the Electricity Act mandates the
Commission to safeguard consumer interests while also ensuring recovery of
cost of electricity in a reasonable manner, whereas Section 61(g) mandates that
Page 10 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
the tariff should progressively reflect the cost of supply. It is settled law that while
protection of consumer interest is an important consideration, the same cannot
override the generator’s entitlement to recovery of its legitimate costs, as noted
in “Punjab State Power Corpn. Ltd. v. PSERC”, (2015) 7 SCC 387 & “BSES
Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.”,
(2023) 4 SCC 788.
21. It is submitted that under the cost-plus tariff regime, all input costs relating
to generation, including Capex and Opex, are ordinarily treated as pass-through
components in tariff, subject to prudence check by the Commission. This
Tribunal, in various judgments, has held that tariff is a reflection of the actual cost
and unless any imprudence is established in the manner of incurring cost, the
expenditure claimed by the generating company under Section 62 of the
Electricity Act 2003 should be allowed and passed through in tariff, as also held
in “NTPC v. CERC” 2009 ELR (APTEL) 916.
22. Accordingly, in the absence of any imprudence by HPPCL in obtaining the
loan, HPERC ought to have treated the GoHP Loan as a ‘loan’ and not as a ‘Grant’
and allowed the same to be recovered through tariff. However, on account of the
Impugned Orders, HPPCL is not allowed to recover the cost of its generation,
which is contrary to the principles of project-specific cost-reflective tariff
determination under Sections 61 and 62.
23. Learned counsel for the Appellant stated that the Allocation of funds either
by way of Grant or loan is a policy decision of the government. HPERC, exercising
powers under Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, has no jurisdiction to question
or sit in appeal over a policy decision taken by the government. It is a settled
position of law that the Courts cannot interfere with policy decisions of the
government, including decisions relating to allocation of funds and resources and
Page 11 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
grant of loans, which fall under policy domain of the government, as held in
following judgments; Balco Employees Union (Regd) vs. UOI & Ors, (2002) 2
SCC 333; Small Scale Industrial Manufactures Asso. v. UOI, (2021) 8 SCC
511; Rahul Mohod v. Govt. of NCT Delhi & Ors., 2023 SCC OnLine Del 5492;
Judgement dated 19.12.2024 in Appeal No. 284 of 2018 titled Green Infra Wind
Solutions Ltd. v. APERC & Ors.
24. HPPCL is suffering grave and irreparable loss on account of the Impugned
Orders, inasmuch as the reduction in the approved Capital Cost pursuant to
deduction of 90% of the loan amounts has rendered HPPCL incapable of
operating the projects and servicing its debt obligations towards the GoHP at the
tariff approved by the HPERC and as a consequence thereof, HPPCL is facing a
projected annual financial shortfall of approximately Rs. 114.31 Crore.
Submissions Urged on behalf of State Commission - Respondent No.1
25. It is submitted that the common question of law involved in the present
Appeals pertains to the loan arrangement executed between the Asian
Development Bank and the Government of India for the purpose of encouraging
investment and promoting development in special category States such as
Himachal Pradesh, wherein it was stipulated that 90% of the financial assistance
would be treated as grant and the remaining 10% would be treated as loan.
However, Govt of Himachal Pradesh has provided the said amount to the
Appellant as loan.
26. State Commission upon consideration of the funding structure of the
project, was of the view that since the loan assistance received from the Asian
Development Bank by the State of Himachal Pradesh was structured as 90%
Page 12 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
grant and 10% loan, the State of Himachal Pradesh ought to adopt the same
methodology while extending such financial assistance, in the interest of the
consumers of the State. It is submitted that the said Order was passed on a
provisional basis with liberty granted to the Appellant to renegotiate the terms with
the State of Himachal Pradesh and, in the event of any difficulty, to approach the
replying Commission afresh. Thereafter, the Appellant filed Review Petitions
before the replying Commission; however, the same were dismissed as not
maintainable.
ANALYSIS & DISCUSSION
27. The issue under consideration in all the three appeals is confined to a
narrow compass, namely, whether the State Commission was justified in treating
the loan advanced by the Government of Himachal Pradesh to the Appellant for
the three hydro projects as a grant, and consequently deducting the said amount
from the capital cost for tariff determination.
28. It is to note that on 10.09.2008, a Framework Financing Agreement (“FFA”)
was executed between Asian Development Bank, (ADB) and the Government of
India (GoI), wherein a loan of USD 800 million multi-tranche loan was sanctioned
to GoI for the construction of four HEPs namely, Kashang, Sainj, Sawra Kuddu
and Shongtong-Karcham under Himachal Pradesh Investment Program
(“Investment Program”). Thereafter, on 10.11.2008, 12.03.2010, 17.01.2011 and
19.11.2012, GOI and ADB entered into various loan agreement for the
disbursement of the sanctioned loan amount in the four tranches for a principal
repayment period of 20 years, at interest rate of LIBOR+ 0.60%, Less applicable
credit. Tranche 1 and Tranche 2 covered Kashang and Sawra Kuddu HEPs,
while Tranche 3 covered Sainj and Kashang Stage-II & III.
Page 13 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
29. A Loan Agreement “ On Lending Arrangement “ signed between Govt of
Himachal Pradesh and the Appellant on 29.11.2009, also stipulates that Govt Of
India is taking a loan of 800 million US dollar from ADB for development of four
hydro projects in Himachal Pradesh including above referred three projects (
Sawara Kuddu- 111 MW, Keshang 195 MW and Sainj HEP 100 MW). The loan
agreement stipulates that the Govt of India shall transfer the loan to Govt of
Himachal Pradesh and which inter-alia will transfer the same to the Appellant. It
is very clear from the loan agreement that funds so given shall be in the form of
loan carrying simple interest @ 10 % per annum. Para 3 &4 of the loan agreement
are reproduced hereunder :
“3. The second party hereby agrees that the funds so received shall
be in the form of loan carrying simple interest @10% per annum. The
interest will be payable annually on 15th January of each calendar
year and payment of interest will start immediately. The interest will
be calculated from the date of transfer/release of money by first party
to the second party.
4. The second party agrees to repay principle amount of each
tranch of the loan on annual installment basis in 10 years period
starting after initial five years (i.e. grace period) after the signing of the
loan agreement of that particular tranch in total 10 equated
installments payable on 15th January of each calendar year.”
30. Thus, it is apparent that funds so received from ADB to Govt of India has
been extended to the Appellant by Govt of Himachal Pradesh as interest bearing
loan for the implementation of referred projects with repayment liability and
interest payment liability.
31. It is further pertinent to note from the Power Purchase Agreements
executed between the Appellant, HPSEBL and the respective Hydro Electric
Projects on 29.03.2023, that the tariff payable for supply of electricity from these
Page 14 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
projects shall be governed by the Tariff Regulations, Notifications, Orders and
Directions issued or to be issued by the Himachal Pradesh Electricity Regulatory
Commission from time to time. Significantly, our attention has not been drawn to
any provision or stipulation in the said Agreements which makes the purchase of
electricity contingent upon the Appellant availing any grant from the Government
of Himachal Pradesh for implementation of the projects. The contractual
framework thus reinforces that the tariff determination is to be regulated strictly in
accordance with the statutory instruments of the Commission, and not subject to
any extraneous condition of grant funding.
32. The State Commission, while adjudicating upon the tariff petitions filed in
respect of the subject hydro projects, has recorded their findings in the respective
Impugned Orders. For the sake of brevity, and since the reasoning adopted
therein is materially similar, the observations as contained in the Impugned Order
pertaining to Kashang–I Hydro Electric Project are reproduced herein as
representative. The said extract is set out below, and the same may be read
mutatis mutandis in relation to the other projects under consideration.”
“3.8.16 The Commission takes serious note against consideration of
the amount which is available as grant (90% of overall amount) to
the State as loan which shall unnecessarily burden the consumers
of the State due to such treatment. It is also observed that the
Petitioner is already facing financial challenges and has been unable
to service the loans against which deferment has been sought time
and again. The Commission feels that it would be prudent that the
Petitioner takes up the matter with the GoHP regarding restructuring
of the loan amount availed against the project on same terms and
conditions as envisaged under the original scheme of funding i.e.,
90% of the amount to be converted to grant. This would be in interest
of the utility as well as the consumers of the State which would have
to bear the burden of the additional interest cost and repayment of
such loan which has been provided as grant.

3.8.17 Accordingly, the Commission has provisionally considered the
debt amount availed under the ADB scheme as 90% grant and 10%
debt. Further, after reducing such amount of grant from the total
approved capital cost, the Commission has consider debt: equity as
70:30 for the balance amount in line with Regulation 10(C) of the
HPERC Tariff Regulations, 2011 which specify the following:
"(b) the debt to equity ratio shall be considered in accordance with
Regulation 16, after deducting the amount of financial support
provided through consumer contribution, deposit work, capital
subsidy or grant;"
33. Accordingly, after considering 90 % of loan as Grant and deducting it from
the total approved project cost approved, balance cost was apportioned as Debt
70 % and equity 30 %, for the purpose of determination of tariff for all the three
HEPs,

34. In our view, the Commission’s approach of re-characterizing the loan as a
grant, merely on the premise that a substantial portion of the upstream funding
Page 16 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
from GoI to GoHP was in the nature of grant, is legally untenable. The
Commission cannot disregard the binding contractual framework and substitute
its own characterization of the transaction. Such deduction from capital cost is
contrary to the On-Lending Agreement, and amounts to an error apparent on
the face of the record.
35. It has been brought to our notice that subsequent to passing of the
Impugned Order, Appellant had approached GoHP vide its letter dated
12.12.2024, to either consider passing of ADB loan as 90 % grant and 10 % loan
or issue necessary direction to State Commission under Section 108 to consider
terms and Conditions of “on lending Agreement”. Govt. of Himachal Pradesh
vide its letter dated 19.03.2025 conveyed its regret to pass on the ADB loan as
90 % grant to the HPPCL. Thus, there is no doubt that as of now the fund
extended for the implementation of these projects by GoHP are to be treated as
loan with liability of payment of interest and repayment of loan on the Appellant
as per ‘On lending Agreement”.
36. It is of relevance to advert to the Himachal Pradesh Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions for Determination of Hydro Generation Tariff)
Regulations, 2011 (“Hydro Regulation 2011”). The scheme of the Regulations
provides that the capital cost deployed in a project, after prudence check by the
State Commission, shall be considered in the ratio of 70% loan and 30% equity,
where actual equity deployed exceeds 30%, and not more than 30% equity
otherwise. The Regulations further stipulate that capital works undertaken by a
generating company utilizing grants received from the State or Central
Government, including funds received under various schemes, shall be classified
under the category of “Grants.” Regulation 10(C)(3) clarifies that capital works

carried out with funds of similar nature, or amounts received without any
obligation to return the same and carrying no interest liability, shall likewise be

37. Admittedly, the funds received by the Appellant for implementation of the
projects from the Government of Himachal Pradesh do not fall within any of the
categories contemplated under Regulation 10(C)(3). The financing arrangement
is in the form of a loan, carrying a contractual liability of repayment together with
interest at 10% per annum. Such funds cannot, by any interpretative device, be
re-characterized as grants.
38. Thus, treating the loan as grant on the premise that since Govt. of India
extended the ADB funds by way of grants to GoHP and the same should have
been extended by GoHP to the Appellant as Grant, is devoid of legal and
regulatory basis.”, On such erroneous premise, the State Commission proceeded
to reduce the admissible capital cost by the corresponding amount. This
approach is contrary to the express provisions of the Hydro Tariff Regulations,
2011, which mandate that, save and except for capital works financed through
grants, the capital cost is to be considered in the debt: equity ratio of 70:30, with
equity capped at maximum 30 %. Significantly, the Regulations do not contain
any provision permitting a loan, even provisionally, as grant, with corresponding
reduction in capital cost for determination of tariff. State Commission has not
referred to any provisions in the Regulations to this effect.
39. The methodology adopted by the State Commission in the Impugned Order,
whereby the loan advanced by the Government of Himachal Pradesh has been
provisionally treated as grant, is in clear contravention of the statutory framework.
Section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 mandates that while determining tariff, the

Commissions shall ensure that generation, transmission and supply of electricity
are conducted on commercial principles. The Commission is duty-bound to
safeguard consumer interests, but equally to ensure recovery of the legitimate
cost of electricity in a reasonable manner, with tariff progressively reflecting the
actual cost of supply. This has been categorially held by Hon’ble Supreme Court
in “Punjab State Power Corpn. Ltd. v. PSERC”; (2015) 7 SCC 387 & “BSES
Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors”;,
(2023) 4 SCC 788).
40. Tariff determination under Section 62 of the Act requires the Commission to
consider the total debt employed for construction of the project on the basis of
the loan agreements executed between the generating company and its lender,
subject to the debt-equity ratio prescribed under the applicable tariff regulations.
41. By treating the loan received for implementation of the projects as 90%
grant, the Commission has artificially lowered the tariff, thereby jeopardising the
Appellant’s ability to discharge its contractual obligations of servicing interest and
repaying principal under the Loan Agreement with the Government of Himachal
Pradesh.
42. While, the protection of consumer interest remains a paramount objective
under given framework, the same cannot be invoked to defeat or curtail a
generator’s statutory right to recover its legitimate costs. In a regulated regime,
the Commission is bound to act strictly in accordance with the governing
provisions of the Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. The Commission
cannot, under the guise of advancing consumer interest, disregard or deviate
from the express regulatory framework governing tariff determination. Any
departure from the prescribed mechanism can only be effected by way of a formal
amendment to the Regulations in accordance with law, and not otherwise.

43. We are in agreement with the submissions of the Appellant that allocation
of funds either by way of grant or loan is a policy decision of the Government.
The State Commission, exercising powers under Section 86 of the Act, has no
jurisdiction to question such policy decisions. It is a settled position of law that
Courts and Tribunals cannot interfere with policy decisions of the Government,
including those relating to allocation of funds and resources or grant of loans,
which fall squarely within the policy domain. The reliance has been placed on
(“Balco Employees Union (Regd.) vs. UOI & Ors”; (2002) 2 SCC 333, “Small
Scale Industrial Manufactures Asso. v. UOI”; (2021) 8 SCC 511; “Rahul
Mohod. v. Govt. of NCT Delhi & Ors”; 2023 SCC OnLine Del 5492), wherein it
has been observed that the court have consistently refrained from interfering with
economic decisions unless the economic decisions are violative of constitutional
or legal limits. In other words, it is not the court/tribunal duty to consider relative
merits of economic framework and to consider whether a wiser or better one can
be evolved. The issue, if any, of the Government of Himachal Pradesh passing
of funds received from the Government of India as loan to the Appellant is an
inter-se matter between the two Governments and the State Commission has no
jurisdiction to re-characterize such funds as grant for the purpose of Tariff
determination.
44. Accordingly, issue of treatment of loan as Grant and corresponding
reduction in Capital Cost cannot be sustained in law.
CONCLUSION
In view of the foregoing deliberations and findings, we hold that the Impugned
Orders of the State Commission, insofar as it treats 90% of the loan advanced by
